subject: playwright
title: Auto-waiting
description: What actionability actually checks, why waitForTimeout is the wrong tool, and the two waits you still need.

content.title: Actionability
content.body: Before every action Playwright waits for the element to be attached, visible, stable (no animation), able to receive events (nothing covering it) and, for inputs, enabled. Only when all of them hold does the click happen — and if they never do, the error names the check that failed.

content.title: What replaces a sleep
content.body: A fixed timeout is a guess: too short on CI, wasted seconds locally. A web-first assertion waits for the condition you actually care about.

content.title: Watch out
content.body: Auto-waiting covers the element, not your application's state. A spinner that has disappeared does not mean the list finished re-rendering — assert on the data you expect, not on the absence of the loader.

exercises.question: Which of these does Playwright NOT wait for before clicking?

answers.text: The element being stable — no ongoing animation
Every pending network request to finish

exercises.explanation: Network idle is not part of actionability, and waiting for it is usually a mistake — an app with polling or analytics never goes idle.

exercises.question: This test is flaky on CI and passes locally. What is the real problem?

answers.text: Line 1 — click should be awaited twice
Lines 2–4 — a fixed sleep plus a non-retrying assertion on a snapshot count

exercises.explanation: count() reads once, so expect(number) cannot retry. await expect(page.getByRole('row')).toHaveCount(4) polls until the row appears and needs no sleep at all.

exercises.question: Why can the second line never retry?
exercises.code:
const text = await page.getByTestId('total').textContent();
expect(text).toBe('120.00 PLN');

answers.text: textContent() resolves once, so the assertion compares a plain string
toBe never retries by design, but toEqual would
It does retry — expect is always web-first

exercises.explanation: Retrying is a property of asserting on a *locator*: await expect(page.getByTestId('total')).toHaveText('120.00 PLN') re-reads until it matches or the timeout expires.

exercises.question: waitForLoadState('networkidle') is the recommended way to wait for a single-page app to settle.
exercises.explanation: The Playwright docs discourage it. Polling, websockets or analytics keep the network busy forever; assert on something the user can see instead.

exercises.question: You need the click and the request it triggers to be awaited together, without a race. Complete the call.
exercises.explanation: Start the wait before the action, then await it after — that ordering is what avoids missing a fast response. Awaiting waitForResponse before the click would deadlock.

exercises.question: A click times out with "element intercepts pointer events". What does that mean?

answers.text: The element is hidden behind something — a toast, a modal backdrop, a sticky header
The page navigated during the click

exercises.explanation: Playwright hit-tests the point it is about to click. force: true skips the check and usually just moves the failure somewhere less obvious — wait for the overlay to go instead.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Passing force: true to click() skips the ___ checks.
exercises.explanation: It clicks at the coordinates regardless of visibility or interception. Useful for testing a deliberately blocked control; a liability everywhere else.

exercises.question: Which assertion actually proves the list has loaded?

answers.text: B — it asserts on the data, not on the absence of a loader
A — the spinner disappears exactly when loading ends

exercises.explanation: A passes before the spinner ever appears, and again in the gap between the fetch resolving and the rows rendering. Assert the end state you care about.

exercises.question: Playwright · configuration
exercises.back: 5 s per web-first assertion, 30 s for the whole test — tuned separately
exercises.explanation: Raise expect.timeout in the config for a genuinely slow condition; raising the test timeout only hides where the time went.

exercises.topic: When an explicit wait is right
exercises.question: Which case genuinely needs an explicit wait rather than an assertion?

answers.text: Waiting for a button to become enabled
Capturing a network response or a download triggered by an action
Waiting for a row count to settle

exercises.explanation: Everything visible is covered by a retrying assertion. Events that are not part of the DOM — responses, downloads, popups, console messages — need waitFor* started before the action.

exercises.question: Playwright will click an element that is still sliding into place.
exercises.explanation: Stability is an actionability check: it waits for the bounding box to stop moving across two consecutive animation frames, which is what prevents clicks landing next to a toast.

exercises.question: This occasionally fails with "execution context was destroyed". Why?

answers.text: Line 3 — toContain does not work on strings
Line 2 — it reads the title mid-navigation, before the new document exists
Nothing — this is a Playwright bug

exercises.explanation: await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/Reports/) retries across the navigation. One-shot reads taken right after a click are a classic source of CI-only flakiness.
